carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: No deviations were noted when compared with orienting with the compass more distant from the dike. They were sliced to a standard length in the laboratory, most commonly giving one core per sample. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the cores was measured using a "Digico complete results magnetometer" interfaced with a Digital MINC com­ puter. There was a considerable range in the intensity of NRM ranging from values of 8 x 104 ntAm"! to about 1.3 x 108 rrtAm"! in the basic dikes, to a maximum of 1.5 x 10- 4 mAm"! in the intermediate dikes, down to 1 x 10-3 to 3 X 10- 1 rrtAm"! in the acidic rocks. Pro­ gressive alternating field demagnetization of the natural remanent magnetization in a Schonstedt GSD-1 was carried out in 5 mTsteps to 25 mT, above that at 35, 50, 75 and 100 mT on two pilot cores per site (Fig. 3). Thermal demagnetization using the Schonstedt TD was carried out on some samples. The first stages of heating were generally at widely spaced intervals begin­ ning at 200°C and then at 100°C steps, but as higher temperatures were reached the interval was reduced to 50°C (Fig. 4). Programs available on the MINC allowed us to calcu­ late the usual statistical parameters and to compute the vector of the magnetization removed between progres­ sive demagnetization steps. This proved necessary in some samples which have superposed magnetic vectors.

DISCUSSION OF RESULTS (1) Directions of remanence The measurements of the direction of remanence during progressive demagnetization permit us to distin­ guish three patterns of behaviour. For most of the acid and basic dikes examined, and about half of the ande­ sites, after the elimination of a small viscous component there appeared to be but a single component, for the direction of magnetization remained virtually unchanged during demagnetization. This behaviour is illustrated through stable end point curves (Figs 5 and 6) and is the same whether alternating field or thermal techniques were applied. These curves also illustrate the point that in some samples the directions of magnetiza­ tion do not always decay exactly toward the origin, although the directions of magnetization are identical to those of other samples from the same site which do. In some cases an improvement occurred when thermal treatment was applied to samples demagnetized in alter­ nating fields (BM 372, Fig. 7). (Received 27 March 1984) Abstract-Two oppositely directed secondary directions of magnetization were isolated from some of the dikes in the Esh El Mellaha Range. Radiometric and paleomagnetic age considerations suggest that these were acquired during an interval of low-grade metamorphism in late Cambrian time (approx. 530 m.y.), The paleopole position for the acidic dikes (three sites) is 87.3N 25.9E dp 9.6, dm 14.5, for the intermediate dikes (eight sites) 8I.6N 120.8E dp 3.3 dm 5.2 and for the basic dikes (11 sites) 82.7N 86.5W dp 5.6 dm 9.1. INTRODUCTION THE ESH EL MELLAHA Range forms a long, low and narrow range of hills which run parallel to the Red Sea margin. They extend for about 75 km from south of Ras Gharib to just north of Hurghada (Fig. 1) and at their broad

or the boundary faults are mapped along only part of the length of the range (Fig. 2). The principal geological works on the Esh EI Mellaha Range are by Kabesh and Shahin (1968), Kabesh et al. (1970a,b) and Lotfi Abdel-Khalek and Hafez (1973). Basement rocks crop out mainly in the eastern part of the range where there are isolated Miocene outliers. The western part is mantled by Cretaceous and younger sediments (Fig. 2). Good exposures of the rocks of basement complex are found in many of the wadis which cross the range from southwest to northeast, in particular the wadis EI Mellaha, Dib, Abu Had and Betih. The basement rocks are cut by many dikes. Kabesh and Shahin (1968) recorded 500, but that is a minimum. Although the authors recognized about 62 petrological types, they were able to group them as acid, inter­ mediate, alkaline and basic in a generalized oldest to youngest age sequence based upon cross-cutting relationships. A suite of the dikes was collected during the 1980 field season as part of a project of studying the minor intru­ sions of the Eastern Desert with interest centred around the possibility of using the relative age sequence to provide pole positions for successive time intervals which could be compared with dike data presented by Nairn et al.
